title: Random Sampling and Inferences
seo_title: Grade 7 Random Sampling Worksheets: Populations, Biased Samples and Making Inferences
standard_text: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population; generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population. Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest.
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 random sampling worksheets: populations and samples, random versus biased samples, estimating a population from a sample, variation between samples, and making inferences. 100 practice questions with an answer key.
key_big: A random sample gives everyone the same chance. Use its fraction to estimate the whole population.
key_sub: 18 of 50 sampled walk, so about 18/50 × 800 = 288 of 800 students walk. Bigger random samples are more reliable.
body_html:
Populations and samples

A population is the whole group you want to learn about. A sample is the part you actually ask. A random sample gives everyone the same chance to be chosen, so it tends to represent the population.

WordMeaningExample
PopulationThe whole groupAll 800 students
SampleThe part you study80 students
Random sampleEveryone has an equal chanceNames drawn from a list of all students
Biased sampleFavors some answersOnly the soccer team

Estimate with a sample

Find the fraction or percent in the sample, then multiply by the population.

Example

In a random sample of 50 students, 18 walk to school. About how many of 800 students walk?

18 out of 50 = 0.36.

0.36 × 800 = 288.

Answer: about 288 students

Different random samples give slightly different results. Larger samples, and several samples, give more reliable estimates.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting a sample that is easy to reach, like your friends or one club.
  • Using the sample number as the answer for the whole population.
  • Thinking an estimate is an exact value.

faq.q: What is the difference between a population and a sample?
faq.a: The population is the whole group you want to know about. The sample is the smaller group you actually study.
A sample is biased when some members are more likely to be chosen, like asking only the soccer team about favorite sports, or asking a question that pushes people to one answer.

faq.q: How do you estimate a population from a sample?
faq.a: Find the fraction or percent in the sample and multiply it by the population. 12 of 40 is 30%, so about 30% of 500 = 150.

faq.q: Why do different samples give different results?
faq.a: Each random sample includes different people, so results vary a little. Larger samples vary less.

items.q: A school wants to know its 800 students' favorite lunch. It asks 80 students. What is the population?
c: the people who run the survey
only the students who like pizza
items.e: The population is the whole group you want to learn about: all 800 students.

items.q: A school wants to know its 800 students' favorite lunch. It asks 80 students. What is the sample?
c: the answers that were most common
items.e: The sample is the part of the population you actually study: the 80 students asked.

items.q: A factory checks 50 of the 2,000 light bulbs it made today. What is the population?

items.e: The population is the whole group you want to learn about: all 2,000 light bulbs made today.

items.q: A factory checks 50 of the 2,000 light bulbs it made today. What is the sample?
c: the answers that were most common
items.e: The sample is the part of the population you actually study: the 50 bulbs checked.

items.q: A town surveys 300 of its 12,000 voters about a new park. What is the population?
c: the people who run the survey
items.e: The population is the whole group you want to learn about: all 12,000 voters.

items.q: A town surveys 300 of its 12,000 voters about a new park. What is the sample?
c: the answers that were most common
items.e: The sample is the part of the population you actually study: the 300 voters surveyed.

items.q: A biologist catches 40 fish from a lake to study their size. What is the population?
c: all the fish in the lake
the people who run the survey
items.e: The population is the whole group you want to learn about: all the fish in the lake.

items.q: A biologist catches 40 fish from a lake to study their size. What is the sample?
c: all the fish in the lake
the answers that were most common
items.e: The sample is the part of the population you actually study: the 40 fish caught.

items.q: What is a random sample?
c: A sample of the people who are easiest to reach
A sample where every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen
A sample chosen by the teacher's favorite students
items.e: In a random sample, everyone has the same chance, so the sample tends to represent the population.

items.q: Why do we use samples instead of asking everyone?
c: Samples do not need to be random
Asking everyone can take too much time or cost too much
items.e: A good sample gives a useful estimate with much less work.

items.q: What is a biased sample?
c: A sample that does not represent the population well
A sample that is too large
items.e: A biased sample favors some answers, so its results can be misleading.

items.q: Which word means the sample represents the population?
items.e: A representative sample has the same kinds of members as the population.

items.q: A larger random sample usually gives…
items.e: Bigger random samples vary less from the population.

items.q: Two random samples from the same population give slightly different results. Is that normal?
c: No, the survey must be wrong
Yes, random samples vary a little
Only if the samples are biased
items.e: This is called sampling variability. Results should be close, not identical.

items.q: A sample is used to make a guess about the whole population. This guess is called…
items.e: Using a sample to draw a conclusion about a population is making an inference.

items.q: Asking every member of the population is called…
items.e: A census collects data from the whole population.

items.q: A sample of 10 people out of 50,000 is…
c: biased only if they are adults
probably too small to be reliable
items.e: Very small samples can give results far from the population.

items.q: Which helps make a sample random?
c: Drawing names from a hat with every name in it
Asking people who walk by first
items.e: Every name has an equal chance in a fair drawing.

items.q: A study looks at 500 randomly chosen high school students in Ohio. Which population can it describe best?
c: All people in the United States
items.e: A sample can only describe the population it was chosen from.

items.q: What is a numerical fact about a sample, such as its mean, called?
items.e: A statistic describes a sample. It is used to estimate a value for the population.

items.q: To find the favorite sport at school, Leo asks the soccer team. Is the sample random or biased?

Random: every student could be asked
Biased: the team is too large
Biased: the soccer team likes soccer more than most students
items.e: Ask: does every member of the population have the same chance to be chosen?

items.q: Which is the best way to find out what all 600 students want for a class trip?

Ask the first 60 students in line for lunch

items.e: A good sample is random and from the whole population, and the question does not push people toward an answer.

items.q: Which sample best represents the people in a town?

90% is too high to be possible

sets.title: Estimate a population from a sample

items.q: In a random sample of 40 students, 12 like rock music. There are 500 students in all. About how many like rock music?
items.e: 12 out of 40 is 12/40. Multiply by the population: 12/40 × 500 = 150.

items.q: In a random sample of 50 students, 18 walk to school. There are 800 students in all. About how many walk to school?
items.e: 18 out of 50 is 18/50. Multiply by the population: 18/50 × 800 = 288.

items.q: In a random sample of 60 voters, 15 support the plan. There are 1,200 voters in all. About how many support the plan?
items.e: 15 out of 60 is 15/60. Multiply by the population: 15/60 × 1,200 = 300.

items.q: In a random sample of 80 people, 20 own a bike. There are 2,000 people in all. About how many own a bike?
items.e: 20 out of 80 is 20/80. Multiply by the population: 20/80 × 2,000 = 500.

items.q: In a random sample of 25 bulbs, 4 are broken. There are 750 bulbs in all. About how many are broken?
items.e: 4 out of 25 is 4/25. Multiply by the population: 4/25 × 750 = 120.

items.q: In a random sample of 100 fans, 35 buy a T-shirt. There are 3,000 fans in all. About how many buy a T-shirt?
items.e: 35 out of 100 is 35/100. Multiply by the population: 35/100 × 3,000 = 1,050.

items.q: In a random sample of 30 students, 9 play an instrument. There are 450 students in all. About how many play an instrument?
items.e: 9 out of 30 is 9/30. Multiply by the population: 9/30 × 450 = 135.

items.q: In a random sample of 200 phones, 14 have a problem. There are 5,000 phones in all. About how many have a problem?
items.e: 14 out of 200 is 14/200. Multiply by the population: 14/200 × 5,000 = 350.

items.q: In a random sample of 75 students, 30 prefer pizza. There are 900 students in all. About how many prefer pizza?
items.e: 30 out of 75 is 30/75. Multiply by the population: 30/75 × 900 = 360.

items.q: In a random sample of 40 shoppers, 26 use a list. There are 600 shoppers in all. About how many use a list?

items.q: In a random sample of 20 students, 7 read every day. There are 360 students in all. About how many read every day?
items.e: 7 out of 20 is 7/20. Multiply by the population: 7/20 × 360 = 126.

items.q: In a random sample of 50 people, 30 chose blue as their favorite color. What percent of the sample is that?
In a random sample of 40 people, 10 chose blue as their favorite color. What percent of the sample is that?
In a random sample of 80 people, 52 chose blue as their favorite color. What percent of the sample is that?
In a random sample of 200 people, 46 chose blue as their favorite color. What percent of the sample is that?
Rangers tag 50 deer and let them go. Later they see 200 deer, and 5 are tagged. About how many deer live in the park?
items.e: 5 of 200 seen are tagged, so tagged deer are 5/200 of all deer. 50 ÷ (5/200) = 2,000.

items.q: Rangers tag 30 deer and let them go. Later they see 60 deer, and 6 are tagged. About how many deer live in the park?
items.e: 6 of 60 seen are tagged, so tagged deer are 6/60 of all deer. 30 ÷ (6/60) = 300.

items.q: Rangers tag 40 deer and let them go. Later they see 80 deer, and 4 are tagged. About how many deer live in the park?
items.e: 4 of 80 seen are tagged, so tagged deer are 4/80 of all deer. 40 ÷ (4/80) = 800.

items.q: Rangers tag 100 deer and let them go. Later they see 150 deer, and 10 are tagged. About how many deer live in the park?
items.e: 10 of 150 seen are tagged, so tagged deer are 10/150 of all deer. 100 ÷ (10/150) = 1,500.

items.q: Four random samples of 50 students gave these numbers who like hiking: 12, 15, 13, 14. What is a good estimate for one sample of 50?
items.e: Use the mean of the samples: (12 + 15 + 13 + 14) ÷ 4 = 13.5.

items.q: Four random samples of 50 students gave these numbers who like hiking: 22, 25, 20, 23. What is a good estimate for one sample of 50?
items.e: Use the mean of the samples: (22 + 25 + 20 + 23) ÷ 4 = 22.5.

items.q: Four random samples of 50 students gave these numbers who like hiking: 8, 10, 9, 13. What is a good estimate for one sample of 50?
items.e: Use the mean of the samples: (8 + 10 + 9 + 13) ÷ 4 = 10.
